Amazon sets goal to cut electricity carbon intensity 65% by 2030  
As energy demand grows, Amazon is setting a new, science-aligned interim target for electricity emissions as a leading corporate buyer of carbon-free energy.
Share
Written by 
Kara Hurst
, Chief Sustainability Officer at Amazon
Published:

November 17, 2026
3 min read
Key takeaways
Amazon aims to reduce the carbon emissions for every unit of electricity it uses by 65% by 2030.
The target covers electricity consumed by Amazon’s global operations and follows the International Energy Agency's net-zero pathway.
Amazon has invested in more than 
700 carbon-free energy projects globally
, with capacity to power more than 12.1 million U.S. homes once completed.
When we co-founded 
The Climate Pledge
 in 2019, we committed to reaching 
net-zero carbon emissions by 2040
, knowing that the electricity powering our business would be central to getting there. That's why we’ve built the largest corporate portfolio of carbon-free energy in the world: more than 700 projects globally and over 40 gigawatts of capacity, enough to power more than 12.1 million U.S. homes once completed. Now we’re ready to take the next step.
Today, we’re setting a new goal: By 2030, we aim to cut the carbon intensity of the electricity our global operations use by 65%, compared with 2019. We’re doing this as energy demand rises, because we believe growing our business and cutting emissions can, and must, go hand in hand. Carbon intensity is one of the clearest ways to show that.
Amazon to invest $7 billion in renewable energy in India by 2030
Amazon also announced four new wind and solar projects in India, including its largest wind farm contracted in Asia to date.
We developed this goal and methodology based on the 
International Energy Agency’s Net Zero by 2050
 pathway and reviewed it with leading academics. We commit to updating it so it stays aligned with the latest climate science.
What is carbon intensity and why does it matter?
Carbon intensity tracks emissions per unit of electricity consumed, measured in carbon dioxide equivalent (CO₂e) per megawatt-hour (MWh). Put simply, by 2030 we aim for each unit of electricity we use to be associated with 65% fewer carbon emissions than in 2019. Because it measures progress per unit, it shows whether we’re decarbonizing our electricity supply and decoupling emissions from business growth, however much we grow. 
Electricity demand is rising fast across the technology sector, driven by cloud computing and AI. That’s a challenge for the whole industry. A near-term, measurable goal keeps us focused and gives customers a clear trajectory to track our progress against.
How Amazon approaches carbon credits, a key tool in the fight against climate change
Carbon credits help unlock private sector climate finance at scale, and drive impact beyond our own operations.
How is Amazon investing in carbon-free energy?
Every new carbon-free energy project we bring online can help displace fossil-fuel generation on the grid, lowering the carbon intensity of the electricity we consume. Since 2019, BloombergNEF has consistently recognized us as one of the 
world’s largest corporate purchasers of carbon-free energy
.
Our strategy spans power purchase agreements, utility-scale solar and wind farms, on-site generation, and advanced nuclear and geothermal energy. Together with 
X-energy
, we aim to bring more than 5 gigawatts of new advanced nuclear power online across the U.S. by 2039, the largest commercial deployment target for 
small modular reactors
 to date. We focus in particular on countries where new carbon-free energy can make the biggest impact in 
decarbonizing the grid
. Our announcement this week that we plan to invest $7 billion in renewable energy in India by 2030 further supports this goal.
Amazon’s carbon-free energy projects contribute $11 billion to US GDP, support nearly 22,000 jobs in local communities
Amazon's solar, wind, nuclear, and battery storage investments drove economic growth across the U.S. from 2023 through 2025, per an Oxford Economics study. 
What comes next?
Meeting this goal will mean scaling the carbon-free energy we already invest in and working alongside utilities, grid operators and policymakers to bring more carbon-free power online where we operate. All the while, we’ll seek to ensure these projects benefit local communities.
Through our Built Together initiative in the U.S., we invest in education, job training, energy affordability and 
water preservation
, and fund priorities that communities choose for themselves. This work is guided by the Amazon Data Center Commitment.
We’ll report our progress every year in our Sustainability Report.
Learn more about how Amazon is 
meeting the energy needs of the future
.
We thank Dr. Joe DeCarolis, Department Head and Professor of Engineering and Public Policy at Carnegie Mellon University; Dr. Costa Samaras, Director of the Wilton E. Scott Institute for Energy Innovation at Carnegie Mellon University; Dr. Jeremy Gregory, Executive Director of the MIT Climate and Sustainability Consortium; and Dr. Wenjuan Liu, Climate Intelligence Manager at RMI, for reviewing a draft of this methodology and sharing their feedback, which we considered in preparing this document.
